paragraphs: When they reached Iconium, they did what they always did — went to the Jewish synagogue and shared their message. The message convinced Jews and non-Jews alike, and not just a handful. But the Jews who refused to believe started a whisper campaign against Paul and Barnabas, planting mistrust and suspicion in people's minds. The two apostles stayed a long time anyway, speaking boldly and openly, laying out the clear evidence of God's grace — with God backing up their words through miracles and wonders.

But then the town split — some sided with the Jews, some with the apostles. One day Paul and Barnabas found out that both Jews and non-Jews, egged on by their leaders, were planning to beat them up. So they got out as fast as they could and headed for the next towns — Lystra, Derbe, and the whole Lyconia region. And once they got there, they were right back at it, spreading the message.

In Lystra there was a man who couldn't walk — crippled from the day he was born. He sat there listening to Paul speak, and Paul, looking him straight in the eye, could see he was ready — full of faith that God could work. So Paul said, loud enough for everyone to hear, "Stand up!" The man was on his feet in a flash — jumping up and walking around like he'd been doing it all his life.

When the crowd saw what Paul had done, they went crazy, shouting in their Lyconian language, "The gods have come down to us! These men are gods!" They called Barnabas "Zeus" and Paul "Hermes" (since Paul did most of the talking). The priest of the local Zeus temple organized a parade — bulls, banners, and a crowd lined up right at the gates, ready to offer sacrifices.

When Barnabas and Paul finally figured out what was happening, they rushed in to stop it. Waving their arms, they broke up the parade, shouting, "What are you doing?! We're not gods! We're just men, like you — and we're here to bring you good news, to convince you to ditch these empty god-superstitions and turn to the real thing: God himself, the living God. We don't make God; he makes us — and everything else: sky, earth, sea, and it all."

"In past generations, God let all the nations go their own way. But he never left them without evidence — he made a good creation, sent rain, and gave huge harvests. When your stomachs were full and your hearts were happy, that was proof of goodness beyond anything you did yourselves." They talked fast and hard like that, and just barely stopped the crowd from going through with the sacrifice that would have honored them as gods.

Then some Jews from Antioch and Iconium caught up with them and turned the fickle crowd against Paul and Barnabas. They stoned Paul until he was unconscious, dragged him out of town, and left him for dead. But as the disciples gathered around him, he came to and stood up. He walked back into town — and the next day he left with Barnabas for Derbe.

After preaching the message in Derbe and building a solid core of disciples, they backtracked through Lystra, then Iconium, then Antioch — toughening up the disciples, urging them to hold on to what they'd started believing and not give up. They were straight with them: it wouldn't be easy. "Anyone signing up for God's kingdom has to go through plenty of hard times."

Paul and Barnabas handpicked leaders for each church. After praying — fasting to focus their prayers — they committed these new leaders to the Master they'd entrusted their lives to. Then they worked their way back through Pisidia, came to Pamphylia, and preached in Perga. Finally they reached Attalia and caught a ship back to Antioch, where it had all begun — sent out by God's grace, and now brought safely home by God's grace. A job well done.

When they arrived, they gathered the church and reported on the trip, describing in detail how God had used them to fling the door of faith wide open so people from every nation could stream in. Then they settled in for a nice long visit with the disciples.
title: Road Trip, Riots, and Getting Mistaken for Gods
